::: {.solutions}

**Show all your reasoning.** Total: **32 marks** · Suggested time: **45 minutes**.

Two lines settle every question below:

$$\textbf{“}A \textbf{ sufficient for } B \textbf{”} = A \Rightarrow B \qquad\qquad
\textbf{“}A \textbf{ necessary for } B \textbf{”} = B \Rightarrow A$$

When the wording is reversed (*"a necessary condition for $Q$ is $P$"*), find the **target** — it follows
the word *for* — and the **condition**, then apply the rule.

| Section | What it covers | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Fluency** | translating the two words; deciding in concrete cases | 10 |
| **B — Exam standard** | reversed wording; proving *not sufficient*; equivalence | 14 |
| **C — Stretch** | comparing several conditions; combining both words | 8 |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Also due this session:** Notes on Logic and Proof, **pp. 51–55**, and re-read the complete translation
table in the class material (Question 5's Concepts box).
:::

# Section A — Fluency

## Question 1 **[4]**

$P$ and $Q$ are statements. Write each of the following as an implication.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $Q$ is **sufficient** for $P$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $Q$ is **necessary** for $P$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) A **necessary** condition for $P$ is $Q$. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) Which **two** of (a)–(c) say the same thing? **[1]**

## Question 2 **[3]**

Let $n$ be a positive integer. For each pair, state whether the first condition is **sufficient**,
**necessary**, **both**, or **neither** for the second. Justify each with a proof or a counterexample.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) "$n$ is divisible by $3$" &nbsp;·&nbsp; "$n$ is divisible by $9$" **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) "$n$ is divisible by $2$ and by $5$" &nbsp;·&nbsp; "$n$ is divisible by $10$" **[1]**

## Question 5 **[5]**

$n$ is a positive integer. Consider the theorem

$$\text{If } n \text{ is divisible by } 6, \text{ then } n \text{ is even.} \tag{$*$}$$

Which of the following, **taken individually**, is/are equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; A necessary condition for $n$ to be even is that $n$ is divisible by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; $n$ being divisible by $6$ is sufficient for $n$ to be even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $n$ is odd, then $n$ is not divisible by $6$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None

**Name the halves and show your arrows.** **[5]**

student right? Justify your answer. **[2]**
